messages.subject: Identifying Slope Estimates
parts:
Hello! I am having trouble identifying the slope estimates in my colext() occupancy model, especially when there are multiple categorical covariates. Below I have pasted the model output for my "Regional Detection Probability" model. Which estimates differences in detection probability between the three survey regions.

I need one number which describes the relationship between detection probability and the covariates included in the model. How do I find this, or calculate this?

Code:

> fm3

Call:
colext(psiformula = ~1, gammaformula = ~1, epsilonformula = ~1, 
    pformula = ~unlist(site.region) - 1, data = EagaUMF, se = TRUE)

Initial:
 Estimate    SE   z P(>|z|)
     1.37 0.622 2.2   0.028

Colonization:
 Estimate   SE      z P(>|z|)
    -1.08 1.65 -0.651   0.515

Extinction:
 Estimate    SE     z P(>|z|)
    -1.32 0.712 -1.85  0.0638

Detection:
                       Estimate    SE      z P(>|z|)
unlist(site.region)BP    0.0391 0.300  0.131 0.89609
unlist(site.region)EGB  -0.7576 0.249 -3.042 0.00235
unlist(site.region)SWC  -0.8674 0.319 -2.718 0.00658

AIC: 311.0701

messages.author: f4bebbdb3c5fcabc
messages.subject: Re: Identifying Slope Estimates
parts:
I'm not an "unmarked" specialist so maybe the code developers can further comment on this, but to me it looks like your variables are categorical variables. If your variables is continuous, linear regression is used to get the relationship between the variable and the detection probability - so you get a slope and an intercept. With categorical variables, you get a coefficient for each variable. This can be implemented in different way and I think unmarked uses dummy coding, meaning that one of the categories is taken as the omitted (reference) level. So in your case I assume you have another category besides BP, EGB and SWC, which has thus been taken as the reference level. From a stats website:
"When using dummy coding, the constant is the mean of the omitted level of the categorical variable.  The coefficient for x1 is the difference between the mean of the dependent variable for level 1 of race minus the mean of the dependent variable at level 4 of race (the reference level).  Likewise, the coefficient for x2 and x3 is the mean of the dependent variable at that level of race minus the mean of the dependent variable for the reference level." 

So the Estimates are relative effects - relative to the omitted level/category.

There is thus not one number that describes this relationship. You can get the detection probabilities for each region by running predict() with a dataframe that has your regions (as factors) as input.

Geraldine

messages.author: 67eefb0e32c64fae
messages.subject: Re: Identifying Slope Estimates
parts:
Geraldine,

You are correct. I found the following answer:

·        "By default in R, a factor such as year in this analysis, is a parameterized in terms of an intercept and effects representing differences. This would mean that the parameter for the first year is the intercept and the effects would denote the differences between the parameter values in all other years, relative to the parameter value in the first year, which serves as a reference level. This treatment or effects parameterization is useful for testing for differences. For simple presentation, a means parameterization is more practical. It can be specified by adding a -1 to the formula for the time-dependent parameters."


Sean
